text:
wise words right there / "knows some shit" type tweet...correct sense for the rhythm of life.

touches on 10 random things:

1. quote is like the one from Baltasar Gracian: 

"When one enters into the house of fortune by the gate of pleasure, one leaves it by that of sorrow, and vice versa."

2. the duality of all things.

nothing is as good as it seems, but nothing is as bad as it seems, either...u get it both ways.

and then the relationship/connection/interplay between pain and pleasure -- the removal of todays pleasure, will be what constitutes tomorrow's pain

one of those glaring realities of human nature - u get nothing for free, ever

3. the "harshest defeat"

like what spinoza wrote about how a friend that becomes an enemy, is a far more bitter foe than if the friendship had never existed in the first place.

similarly, the most violent hatred you will ever witness, always existed first in the form of love.

4. losses follow wins

partially as balance, and partially because the W itself was what created the L. 

"Success is a poison that should only be taken late in life and then only in small doses.” - Trollope

alternatively, losses restore equilibrium...the opposites emerge at the poles + duality reigns supreme:

"Prosperity doth discover vice, as adversity doth discover virtue." Bacon

5. sardonic tone

not the perfect word but I get his drift

its the gentle, cynical mocking that becomes instinctual in the face of joy...recognizing that it never lasts, it's all fleeting

you acquire this after massive shifts in fortune, peaks and valleys, pride and shame

and u develop the sage's mix of contempt and apathy for human nature, in all its infinite vanity

the tone is that of Pascal, or Schopenhauer, or Montaigne's essay "Democritus and Heraclitus"

it's never in a bitter way...sardonic is slightly off, more melancholic and amused, but not quite at contempt and scorn

all part of ur very brief tour of planet earth.

6. there is only one fixed and immutable presence 

the sole presence that is guaranteed to be with u from the cradle to the grave. 

that presence is God.

beyond that...everyone and everything in ur life will leave you someday.

they will either leave physically, or they will leave thru death.

7. you accept this impermanence with a warm heart

and u enter new relationships with eyes wide open. nothing changes. u are always receptive to joy, to pleasure, and to love, and u are always willing to risk your heart.

but simultaneously, u are silently laughing to urself. because u must always ponder the balancing act, visualizing the negative scenario

contemplating, at the dawn of a promising new relationship: "man, I cannot fuckin WAIT to see how this one ends."

have to laugh at all of this, and let it roll off ya

8. there is a balance here between pessimism and warmth

its very rare in a human - "old soul" types that are decades wiser than their age.

most people are naive/optimistic/unwilling to face harsh realities. not enough risk, not enough failure, not enough pain...same mindset & attitude as 20 years ago.

others go too far in the other direction and become broken, bitter, resentful, cruel, hateful, envious "victim mentality" types.

those are the extremes to avoid.

9. there is a term from Leopardi, "the courage of philosophical pessimism"

where he cautions, don't attribute my pessimistic outlook to my demeanor or temperament or circumstances...I arrived here through research.

Tolstoy's "Confession" is another good case study, a man on a similar journey to what is being described here -- the emptiness explored by Schopenhauer, King Solomon, Buddha -- and then going the other direction, away from intellectual pessimism, and towards the simple Russian peasant's belief in God...the same final destination every sage and philosopher arrives at.

but that's what the discerning eye can pick up on -- bad negativity/pessimism vs acquired realism + a willingness to call balls and strikes, starting with urself.

the untrained eye just sees something dark, grim, emotionally distant, disturbed, and chalks it up to "circumstance made them that way"

a way to frame it: those who understand and face Jung's "shadow," and those who don't...the 1H/2H dynamics, stuff that Jung disciples like Rohr write about.

go to my pinned tweet, ctrl+f Jung, read parts 1-2.

10. the final goal

you want to develop fluency in suffering, and be fearless and courageous in confronting all the ugliest sides of life...but u don't want to let ur warm heart turn cold in the process.

I cannot give u step-by-step directions on how this is done, mostly because I think 100% of any calibration has been against my will.

the pain/suffering that shape u, and push u towards final form, are involuntary by definition.

the naive archetype remains naive bc avoidance of pain is the primary objective.

but without pain, there is no growth and thus the mind stagnates.

(END)

at some point u have to take a risk, one where there is a real possibility that u are left shattered on the ground, covered in blood and broken glass.

without that risk, there is no chance of progress.

I wish there was a more pleasant answer, but that's reality. u really see it from ages 20 to 40, the people who change and shift and grow and mature...almost entirely a function of pain and suffering.

c'est la guerre

do with this information what u will...and recall:

joseph campbell: "the cave you fear to enter, holds the treasure that you seek."
